```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
tab_col <- c(species = pal[["teal"]], genes = pal[["orange"]])
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
qc <- read_csv(file.path(res, "sample_qc.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(table = factor(table, c("species", "genes")))
fc <- read_csv(file.path(res, "filter_curve.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(table = factor(table, c("species", "genes")))
```

## Yesterday you built a count table out of beads {.center}

Today the same table has 220 rows of bacteria, 14,226 rows of human genes, and
471 columns.

## The files {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)

metadata <- read_csv("data/instructional_dataset/01_metadata.csv")
species  <- read_csv("data/instructional_dataset/02_microbiome_counts.csv")
genes    <- read_csv("data/instructional_dataset/04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz")
```

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  file = c("01_metadata.csv", "02_microbiome_counts.csv", "03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv",
           "04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz", "05_gene_annotation.csv", "06_cytokines.csv"),
  `what it holds` = c("one row per sample: participant, visit, outcome, clinical measures",
                      "220 bacterial species x 471 samples",
                      "what each species is: domain down to species",
                      "14,226 human genes x 471 samples",
                      "what each gene is: Ensembl id, symbol, name",
                      "measured protein concentrations, for the group projects")
) |> kable()
```

## A corner of the species table

```{r}
#| echo: false
read_csv(file.path(res, "corner_species.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  kable()
```

## A corner of the gene table

```{r}
#| echo: false
read_csv(file.path(res, "corner_genes.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  kable()
```

Same shape. Features in rows, samples in columns, counts in the cells.

## Four questions, asked of both tables

::: {.incremental}
1. How deeply was each sample sequenced?
2. How many features did we actually see?
3. How evenly is each sample spread across its features?
4. Which features can we afford to keep?
:::

. . .

Answer those and you have done quality control. Nothing else today.

## 1. How deeply was each sample sequenced?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(qc, aes(library_size, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tab_col) +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "total counts in the sample (log scale)", y = "samples") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Both spread over more than an order of magnitude. Note the axis labels.

## The numbers behind that figure

```{r}
#| echo: false
qc |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(`median library size` = scales::comma(median(library_size)),
            smallest = scales::comma(min(library_size)),
            largest = scales::comma(max(library_size))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

. . .

One sample has 438 bacterial reads. What would you do with it?

## 2. How many features did we see?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
qc |>
  mutate(share = features_detected / features_total) |>
  ggplot(aes(library_size, features_detected, colour = table)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = tab_col) +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "library size (log scale)", y = "features with a count above zero") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

In the species table, how many you see depends on how hard you looked. In the
gene table it does not.

## The same picture as a fraction {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
qc |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(`features in the table` = scales::comma(first(features_total)),
            `median detected` = scales::comma(median(features_detected)),
            `median share detected` = scales::percent(median(features_detected / features_total), 0.1),
            `median cells that are zero` = scales::percent(median(zero_fraction), 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

. . .

The species table is mostly zeros. The gene table is almost solid.

. . .

This single difference drives every filtering decision you will make.

## 3. How evenly is a sample spread?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(qc, aes(top_feature_share, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tab_col) +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "share of the sample held by its single largest feature", y = "samples") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Half of our bacterial samples are more than 60% one species. The most extreme
is 99.9%.

## Richness and evenness, in one number {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# number of features seen, and how evenly the counts are spread
richness <- colSums(counts > 0)
shannon  <- vegan::diversity(t(proportions), index = "shannon")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.1
ggplot(qc, aes(shannon, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = tab_col) +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Shannon diversity", y = "samples") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Species: median `r round(median(qc$shannon[qc$table == "species"]), 2)`. Genes:
median `r round(median(qc$shannon[qc$table == "genes"]), 2)`.

## Be honest about that second number {.center}

Nobody reports Shannon diversity of a transcriptome.

. . .

But "how many features did I detect" and "how evenly are they spread" are
exactly the questions you use to decide **which samples to throw away**, in
both experiments.

. . .

Same question. One field gives it a name and a journal; the other calls it QC.

## 4. Which features can we keep? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# keep a feature if it appears in at least 10% of samples
prevalence <- rowMeans(counts > 0)
kept <- counts[prevalence >= 0.10, ]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.3
fc |>
  pivot_longer(c(features_kept, share_of_counts_kept)) |>
  mutate(name = recode(name, features_kept = "features kept",
                       share_of_counts_kept = "share of all counts kept")) |>
  ggplot(aes(min_prevalence, value, colour = table)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = tab_col) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  facet_grid(name ~ table, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "minimum prevalence required to keep a feature", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Read the bottom left panel again {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
fc |>
  filter(min_prevalence %in% c(0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50)) |>
  transmute(table, `prevalence cutoff` = scales::percent(min_prevalence),
            `features kept` = scales::comma(features_kept),
            `share of counts kept` = scales::percent(share_of_counts_kept, 0.01)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = table, values_from = c(`features kept`, `share of counts kept`)) |>
  kable()
```

::: {.incremental}
- Species: a 10% prevalence filter drops **161 of 220** features and loses
  **0.8%** of the data.
- Genes: the same filter drops **nothing**. Prevalence is the wrong knob here.
:::

## The right filter is not the same filter {.smaller}

| | sparse table (species) | dense table (genes) |
|---|---|---|
| the problem | most features are absent from most samples | nearly everything is present at some level |
| filter on | prevalence | expression level |
| typical rule | present in at least 10% of samples | mean CPM of at least 5 |
| what it buys you | fewer tests, less noise | fewer tests, less noise |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

. . .

Different rule, identical motive.

## You cannot compare raw counts {.smaller}

A sample with twice the library size has roughly twice the count for everything.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# relative abundance: each column sums to 1
proportions <- sweep(counts, 2, colSums(counts), "/")

# counts per million: the same thing, scaled so the numbers are readable
cpm <- proportions * 1e6
```

. . .

Microbiome papers say "relative abundance". RNA-seq papers say "CPM". It is the
same division.

## And then you take a log {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.3
set.seed(4)
x <- rnbinom(4000, mu = 40, size = 0.35)
p1 <- tibble(x) |> ggplot(aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = pal[["navy"]], colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "counts per million", x = NULL, y = NULL)
p2 <- tibble(x) |> ggplot(aes(log2(x + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = pal[["navy"]], colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "log2(counts per million + 1)", x = NULL, y = NULL)
p1 + p2
```

The `+ 1` is there because `log2(0)` is negative infinity. That choice changes
your answer, and you should be able to say why you made it.

## Now the pipeline we will use all week {.smaller}

One helper builds the same object from either table.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(microViz)
source("R/count_tables.R")

species_ps <- as_counts(table = "microbiome")
genes_ps   <- as_counts(table = "rnaseq")
```

. . .

microViz was written for microbiome data. It wants a feature table, a sample
table, and a table saying what each feature *is*.

. . .

A gene annotation is that third table wearing different words, so the same verbs
work on genes.

## The same call, twice {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
species_ps |>
  comp_barplot(tax_level = "Genus", n_taxa = 10, sample_order = "bray")

genes_ps |>
  comp_barplot(tax_level = "symbol", n_taxa = 10, sample_order = "bray")
```

. . .

The first is a figure in every microbiome paper you have read.

. . .

The second is a figure nobody makes, and looking at why not tells you something
real about the two experiments.
